diseases.symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves, becoming corky and distorted. Scabby lesions on fruit surface leading to cracking.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Ascospores released from overwintered leaves in leaf litter during spring rains, carried by air currents.
prevention_steps: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn or shred with a flail mower to speed decomposition.
Prune tree canopies to improve airflow and sunlight penetration.
Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Enterprise, GoldRush, Liberty, Prima).
organic_controls: Apply sulfur or liquid lime-sulfur sprays preventatively prior to rain events during primary infection season.
Apply Bacillus subtilis or potassium bicarbonate sprays.
chemical_controls: Preventative protectants: Captan, Mancozeb (FRAC M04, M03).
Systemic fungicides: DMI fungicides (FRAC 3, e.g., Myclobutanil) or SDHI fungicides (FRAC 7, e.g., Fluopyram) in rotation to avoid resistance.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If leaf lesions cover more than 20% of the canopy before petal fall or if commercial fruit quality is at risk.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tree Fruit Production Guide - Apple Scab (https://extension.psu.edu/apple-scab)
Cornell University Cooperative Extension: Apple Scab Disease Identification and Management (https://cals.cornell.edu)
UC Davis IPM: Apple Scab Management Guidelines (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/apple/apple-scab/)

diseases.symptoms: Frogeye leaf spots (circular brown spots with purple margins). Firm brown rot on fruit starting near calyx, turning black with concentric rings.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Spores splash from dead wood, mummified fruit, and bark cankers during warm rains.
prevention_steps: Prune out dead branches, fire blight cankers, and remove all mummified fruit from the orchard.
Burn or dispose of pruned wood promptly rather than leaving brush piles near orchards.
organic_controls: Copper-based fungicides applied during early season dormancy.
Sulfur sprays during early cover sprays.
chemical_controls: Fungicides: Captan, Thiophanate-methyl, or strobilurin fungicides (FRAC 11) applied from silver tip through cover sprays.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If limb cankers girdle main scaffold branches or cause limb dieback.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on upper leaf surfaces. Raised tubular structures (aecia) on leaf undersides and fruit.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Obligate heteroecious fungus cycling between Eastern red cedar / juniper galls and apple foliage via windborne basidiospores.
prevention_steps: Remove nearby Eastern red cedar / juniper trees within a 1-2 mile radius where feasible.
Remove rust galls (cedar apples) from adjacent landscape junipers before spring rains.
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise).
organic_controls: Liquid sulfur or sulfur-based sprays applied preventatively when cedar galls swell in spring.
chemical_controls: Sterol inhibitor / DMI fungicides (FRAC 3, e.g., Myclobutanil, Tebuconazole) or Strobilurins (FRAC 11) from pink bud through third cover.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If premature defoliation exceeds 30% of tree canopy in consecutive seasons.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Rectangular, brown-to-gray lesions restricted by leaf veins (blocky appearance), merging to cause extensive blighting.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Windblown conidia from infected corn residue on the soil surface.
prevention_steps: Plant resistant corn hybrids.
Rotate with non-host crops (soybean, wheat, alfalfa) for 1-2 years.

organic_controls: Crop rotation and biofungicide seed treatments (Trichoderma spp.).
chemical_controls: Foliar fungicides applied at VT-R1 (tasseling to silking): Strobilurin (FRAC 11, Azoxystrobin, Pyraclostrobin) mixed with Triazole (FRAC 3, Propiconazole, Prothioconazole).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If lesions reach the ear leaf or two leaves below the ear leaf prior to VT/R1 stage.

diseases.symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules (uredinia) scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces, rupturing epidermis with powdery spores.

diseases.symptoms: Tiger-stripe leaf pattern (interveinal yellowing and necrosis with green veins). Dark spots ('measles') on berry skin. Wood shows dark vascular streaking.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Fungal spores enter through pruning wounds and propagate within mature vine wood.
prevention_steps: Prune late in the dormant season when wound healing is rapid.
Apply pruning wound sealants (e.g., acrylic paint with fungicide or biocontrol Trichoderma).
Avoid heavy water stress during hot summer periods.
organic_controls: Biocontrol agent Trichoderma atroviride applied directly to fresh pruning wounds.
chemical_controls: No curative foliar fungicide exists for internal wood rot. Protect pruning wounds with registered wound protectants (e.g., Thiophanate-methyl).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If apoplexy (sudden vine collapse) occurs on high-value vineyard blocks.

diseases.symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottle chlorosis on leaves, yellow shoots, vein corking. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Transmitted by Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) vector and grafting of infected budwood.
prevention_steps: Use certified disease-free nursery trees from enclosed screenhouses.
Eradicate confirmed infected trees promptly to remove pathogen reservoirs.
Control Asian citrus psyllid vector populations rigorously.
organic_controls: Release parasitic wasps (Tamarixia radiata) for biological psyllid suppression.
Horticultural and citrus spray oils to deter psyllid egg-laying.
chemical_controls: Systemic insecticides (e.g., Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam - IRAC 4A) and foliar rotation (Pyrethroids, Spinetoram) targeting psyllid flushes.

diseases.symptoms: Large, dark water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems that expand rapidly. White cottony fungal growth on leaf undersides in high humidity. Tubers develop dry brown rot.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Sporangia and zoospores dispersed long distances by wind and rain splash from infected volunteer potatoes, cull piles, or seed tubers.

organic_controls: Preventative copper sprays applied prior to high-risk weather events.
chemical_controls: Protectants: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil. Targeted oomycide systemics: Mandipropamid (FRAC 40), Fluopicolide (FRAC 43), Cyazofamid (FRAC 21), Propamocarb (FRAC 28).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: Immediately notify local extension upon first sighting; late blight is an aggressive community-wide threat.

organic_controls: Beneficial insect habitat and crop rotation.
chemical_controls: No chemical intervention needed.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: Routine agronomy consulting.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.

diseases.scientific_name: Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea), Golovinomyces cichoracearum
diseases.symptoms: White talcum powder-like circular patches on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, petiole, and stems. Leaves turn chlorotic, senesce, and crisp up.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Conidia are wind-dispersed; does not require free water to germinate, only high relative humidity.
prevention_steps: Plant powdery mildew-resistant cucurbit varieties (PMR cultivars).
Provide adequate plant spacing to facilitate airflow within dense squash foliage.
Avoid excessive nitrogen application.
organic_controls: Horticultural oils, potassium bicarbonate (Armicarb/MilStop), neem oil, or sulfur.
chemical_controls: Targeted fungicides: Quinoxyfen (FRAC 13), Cyflufenamid (FRAC U06), Metrafenone (FRAC 50), DMI (FRAC 3, Difenoconazole) applied preventatively at first sign of white spots.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If powdery mildew covers more than 15% of lower leaf surfaces during early fruit development.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.

diseases.symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purplish-red spots on leaves that coalesce, causing the leaf tissue between spots to turn brown, dry out, and curl up like scorched by fire.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Conidia rain-splashed from infected overwintered leaves onto newly emerging foliage.
prevention_steps: Plant certified disease-free strawberry plugs/runners of resistant cultivars (e.g., Allstar, Earliglow).
Mow and incorporate strawberry foliage immediately after harvest (renovation).
Use straw mulch to prevent soil splashing onto leaves and use drip irrigation.
organic_controls: Copper fungicides applied post-renovation in early autumn or early spring.
chemical_controls: Captan, Thiram, or QoI strobilurin fungicides (FRAC 11, Pyraclostrobin, Azoxystrobin) in spring prior to bloom.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If severe foliage scorching threatens runner production in nursery or perennial beds.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.

diseases.scientific_name: Xanthomonas perforans / X. vesicatoria / X. gardneri
diseases.symptoms: Small, greasy, water-soaked dark brown spots on leaves surrounded by yellow halos. Scabby, raised brown eruptions on tomato fruit.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Splashing water, driving rain, contaminated seed, handling wet plants; enters via stomata and mechanical wounds.
prevention_steps: Use hot-water treated or certified disease-free seed.
Do not work in tomato fields when leaves are wet from dew or rain.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops on a 2-3 year cycle.
organic_controls: Copper bactericides mixed with Bacillus subtilis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
chemical_controls: Fixed copper + Mancozeb tank mix; plant defense activators like Acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If widespread defoliation causes fruit sunscald in commercial plantings.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target pattern) on older lower leaves, leaf yellowing around lesions, progressing upwards.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Spores rain-splashed from infested soil and crop debris; windblown conidia.
prevention_steps: Mulch heavily with straw or plastic to create a barrier between soil and lower leaves.
Stake or cage tomatoes and prune bottom 12-18 inches of leaves to prevent soil splash.
Rotate crops with non-solanaceous species.
organic_controls: Copper octanoate, Bacillus subtilis, and bio-fungicides.
chemical_controls: Protectants: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb (FRAC M05, M03). Systemics: Difenoconazole, Azoxystrobin, Boscalid (FRAC 3, 11, 7).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If early blight reaches mid-canopy before first fruit harvest.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.

diseases.symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale green to dark brown oily lesions on leaves and stems. White fluffy mold on leaf undersides in humid mornings. Fruit develops greasy brown rot.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Sporangia carried miles on cool, moist winds; rain-splashed zoospores.
prevention_steps: Plant resistant varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Magic, Iron Lady).
Destroy infected plants immediately in plastic bags to avoid dispersing spores to neighbors.
Monitor regional late blight tracking maps (e.g., USABlight).
organic_controls: Preventative copper sprays applied prior to cool, rainy disease-favoring weather.
chemical_controls: Mandipropamid (FRAC 40), Fluopicolide (FRAC 43), Cyazofamid (FRAC 21), Chlorothalonil (FRAC M05).
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: Immediately alert university extension or regional crop specialist upon identification.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Pale green to yellowish diffuse spots on upper leaf surface corresponding to velvety olive-green to brown fungal growth on the underside.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Conidia airborne and rain-splashed; primarily a severe problem in high tunnels and greenhouses with high humidity.
prevention_steps: Maximize high-tunnel and greenhouse ventilation using exhaust fans and horizontal airflow.
Increase plant spacing and prune lower suckers to open canopy.
Plant resistant varieties with Cf resistance genes.
organic_controls: Copper fungicides, potassium bicarbonate, or hydrogen dioxide.
chemical_controls: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, Difenoconazole, or Cyazofamid labeled for greenhouse/field tomatoes.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If greenhouse crop loses more than 25% photosynthesizing leaf area.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.

diseases.symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (1.5 - 3 mm) with dark brown borders and pale gray or tan centers containing tiny black specks (pycnidia).
diseases.spread_mechanism: Pycnidiospores extruded in gelatinous tendrils and rain-splashed from overwintered debris and weeds (horsenettle).
prevention_steps: Clean cultivation, weed control (destroy horsenettle and nightshade near fields).
Mulch to prevent soil splash and drip irrigate exclusively.
Rotate away from solanaceous crops for 3 years.
organic_controls: Copper octanoate or copper hydroxide applied at weekly intervals during wet weather.
chemical_controls: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or FRAC 11 (Azoxystrobin) / FRAC 7 (Boscalid) in rotation.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If lower foliage defoliation progresses rapidly toward fruit clusters.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.

diseases.symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on upper leaf surface, delicate fine webbing on leaf undersides, leaves turn bronze, dry out, and drop.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Mites crawl between touching foliage and disperse by ballooning on silk threads in hot, dry, dusty wind.
prevention_steps: Keep farm roadways and perimeters watered to reduce dust, which suppresses natural mite predators.
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids and carbamates that kill beneficial predatory insects.
Maintain adequate crop irrigation to reduce plant water stress.
organic_controls: Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus).
Insecticidal soaps, horticultural mineral oil, or rosemary/neem oil emulsions.
chemical_controls: Selective miticides: Bifenazate (Acramite), Spiromesifen (Oberon), Abamectin (Agri-Mek) with proper surfactant.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If webbing appears on upper canopy or fruit clusters during hot dry spells.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Brown, pinpoint lesions expanding into circular to irregular lesions with concentric light and dark brown rings. Fruit develops sunken brownish lesions.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Conidia windblown and rain-splashed from crop debris and alternative weed hosts.
prevention_steps: Increase row spacing to allow rapid canopy drying.
Prune lower leaves to minimize contact with humidity from soil.
Rotate with non-host crops.
organic_controls: Copper fungicides and biological antagonists.
chemical_controls: FRAC 7 (Fluxapyroxad), FRAC 3 (Difenoconazole), FRAC 11 (Pyraclostrobin), or Chlorothalonil.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If fruit lesions exceed 5% of harvestable fruit.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.

diseases.symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaf margins, prominent yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf margins, severe plant stunting, flower drop, and no fruit set.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Transmitted persistently by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci); not seedborne or mechanically transmitted.
prevention_steps: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tygress, Charger, Red Bounty).
Use 50-mesh insect screening on high tunnels/greenhouses to exclude whiteflies.
Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch to repel migrating whiteflies.
Rogue out infected plants immediately upon early symptom development.
organic_controls: Insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, and release of predatory insects (Delphastus catalinae).
chemical_controls: Target the whitefly vector: Systemic neonicotinoids (Imidacloprid, Dinotefuran - IRAC 4A) at transplant, followed by Cyantraniliprole (IRAC 28), Spiromesifen (IRAC 23), or Pyriproxyfen.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: Report suspected outbreaks in new growing districts to agricultural extension.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.
sources: UC Davis IPM: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus Guidelines
University of Florida IFAS: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus Management (ENY-712)

diseases.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, leaf distortion, 'shoestring' or fern-like leaf narrowing, internal browning (brown wall) of fruit.
diseases.spread_mechanism: Extremely stable virus transmitted mechanically by hands, pruning tools, trellis strings, contaminated seed, and worker clothing.
prevention_steps: Plant certified virus-free seed and resistant cultivars (Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance).
Disinfect hands and tools frequently in 20% non-fat dry milk solution or 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP).
Strictly prohibit tobacco smoking/chewing near tomato plants (tobacco carries mosaic viruses).
Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately; do not compost.
organic_controls: Strict sanitation, milk spray dips for tool and hand decontamination.
chemical_controls: No chemical cure exists for viral infections. Manage through sanitation and genetics.
diseases.when_to_consult_expert: If symptoms appear in seed-production or commercial greenhouse tomato operations.
safety_notes: Always read and strictly follow pesticide product label instructions and pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
Wear required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and respirator mask.
Keep all chemicals out of reach of children and away from livestock and drinking water sources.
Consult your local agricultural extension officer or call Kisan Call Center (1800-180-1551) for certified advice.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tomato Mosaic Virus and Tobacco Mosaic Virus
Cornell Vegetable MD Online: Tobamoviruses of Tomato
